LANESABER

Show drivers what 3 feet looks like.

A bright LED pole that mounts on your rear rack, flips down to mark the passing space drivers owe you, and flips up vertical when you do not need it.

Scroll for the story

Nonverbal, on purpose

It talks to drivers so you do not have to.

Most close passes are not malice. They are a driver guessing where your space ends. LaneSaber ends the guess. The plans and the print files are free, and building one yourself is the heart of this project. If building is not your thing, a kit or a finished one is right there too. Every route is here to lower the barrier to safe cycling, pick the one that fits your life.

  • 3 feet. Drawn in light, at exactly the distance the law asks for.
  • No shouting. No gestures. The pole says it.
  • Soft tip, flexible pole. It bends, and it snaps before anything breaks.

Videos side by side, scroll sideways to watch each one

Why it exists

A pool noodle had the right idea. This finishes it.

Riders have strapped foam noodles to their racks for years to claim a little space. It works, a bit. But a noodle is invisible at night, silent about what it means, and easy to ignore.

LaneSaber is that idea built properly. A fiberglass pole wrapped in bright LEDs, sealed in heat shrink, on a mount that flips between vertical and horizontal. Lit, clear, and impossible to misread at speed, in rain, or after dark.

It gives you back a feeling of control on roads that were not designed with you in mind, and it gives drivers a clear, calm signal instead of a conflict.

Neighbors told her husband Rick her LaneSaber lit up the whole road on her trike.

Trike rider, Rapid City, SD, on her LaneSaber at night

A logging truck hit his LaneSaber north of Leggett and took off the end piece. It scared him, and, he said, it may have saved his life.

Taylor Nichols
Co-host, Bike Talk podcast.

The real answer is better roads.

Protected lanes, safe bypasses, streets designed for people outside cars. That is the fix, and it is coming too slowly. LaneSaber is an interim solution, a way to ride with more peace of mind on the roads we have today, while we keep pushing for the roads we deserve.

Open source, from the start

Given away on day one.

LaneSaber was published free the day it was finished, and it stays that way. Build it. Change it. Make it better. Sell it locally in your own town, no permission needed, no license, no royalty, no need to check back. Once one is rolling in a town, it starts conversations and it starts spreading.

Questions

FAQ

What does the pole do if a car actually hits it?

The end is soft and rubber covered, and the pole is very flexible. It bends out of the way, and if it is hit really hard it will snap before it can hurt the rider or damage the car. That is by design. It states the limit without putting anyone at risk.

What bikes does it fit?

Anything with a rear rack or a rail to mount to. It shines on commuters and cargo bikes, and it adapts well to trikes and recumbents, where the rider sits low and a pole up high makes them visible above car hoods. Vertical, it also works as a follow me marker for group rides and bike buses.

Can I really sell these in my town?

Yes. Build them, sell them locally, keep what you make. No permission needed and no royalty. Local builders making them for their own area is the whole model, it beats shipping poles around the world.

Where do I find a 3D printer?

Check your local library, makerspace, school, or bike co-op, many run printers you can book. Print the parts there for the cost of filament. If that is not an option, order the printed parts from the Etsy shop and assemble at home.

Is this a substitute for safe streets?

No, and it does not pretend to be. It is an interim tool for the roads we have now. Keep advocating for protected lanes and better design. Ride with a little more room in the meantime.

Build page

Build one, two ways

A quick rundown of both builds, with parts lists on one page. Full step by step photos live on Instructables.

Full guide on Instructables

Watch the build, step by step

The five workbench videos live on the How-To Videos tab, in build order, from modifying the kickstand to shrinking the final tube.

LaneSaber Original, the metal build

  1. Start with a WALD 16 inch kickstand, American made, durable, and easily modified.
  2. Drill and bend the kickstand to form the flipping mount.
  3. Mount it upside down on the rear rack or basket rail. When attaching it to a child rail on a cargo bike, it works very well to use P clamps, usually those.
  4. Wrap the fiberglass pole with the LED strip.
  5. Seal the wrap in heat shrink for waterproofing, cap the end with the soft rubber tip.
  6. Wire the battery and switch, mount, test the flip. Vertical to ride in a group, horizontal to mark your 3 feet.

LaneSaber Open Build, 3D printed

Print files in prep

  1. Download the print files when they post here. They are free, always.
  2. Print the parts, or book time on a library or makerspace printer.
  3. No kickstand, no drilling, no bending. The printed mount replaces all of that.
  4. Assemble the mount on your rack, fit the pole, wrap and seal the LEDs as in the metal build.
  5. Remix it. Different bike, different mount idea? Print your own design and share it back.

Print file downloads are in prep and will be linked from this page. Nothing to download yet, check back.

Parts list, shared by both builds

Parts need to be sourced to be customized for your thing. Every bike, rack, and rail is a little different, so source the pole, mount, clamp, and hardware to fit your bike and adjust them as you build.

  • Fiberglass pole, 1/4 inch diameter for the LaneSaber, 3 foot for a cargo basket rail, 4 foot for a center mount. For Party Saber, use a 5/16 inch pole.
  • COB LED strip, red for the safety build. Runs on 5 volt or 12 volt: 5 volt is the standard brightness, and 12 volt is often described as too bright, but it is perfect for those wanting maximum visibility. On Amazon: 12v red LaneSaber and LaneSaber 5v usb.
  • 3/4 heat shrink, tubing to seal and waterproof the wrap.
  • Wiring to connect it all up.
  • Battery pack and switch.
  • Small hardware: bolts, screws, and the little bits that hold it together.
  • Clamp, about $2, plus tape and flag bits to finish.
  • LaneSaber Original only: WALD kickstand for the mount, usually about $16.
  • Open Build only: printed mount parts, plus bolts and springs below.

Costs to keep in mind: WALD kickstand usually about $16, clamp about $2, plus wiring, battery and small hardware.

Finding a pole, bolts, and hardware

  • Pole: source it locally first. Driveway markers and snow markers at the hardware store are the same fiberglass stock. Online multipacks work too, and local sourcing keeps a long pole out of the mail.
  • Bolts and hardware: any hardware store rack hardware bin covers the metal build. Bring the mount with you and test fit.
  • Open Build hardware: List coming The specific bolts and springs for the 3D printed version are being finalized and will be added to this page.

Plans and print files are free. Kits and printed parts, in many configurations, are on Etsy.

Costs page

Where the money goes

No mystery pricing. Here is what the parts cost, what a kit covers, and what the assembly fee pays for. Figures are approximate, parts prices move around.

LaneSaber Original, metal build, parts at retail

PartAbout
LED strip$15
Heat shrink$10 and up
Fiberglass pole$5
WALD kickstand, clamps, wiring, battery, small hardwarethe rest
Total, sourced yourselfabout $60

That is buying one of everything at local stores and online, at retail, with nothing left over. Builders who make several at once do better on every line.

LaneSaber Open Build

  • Print files: free to download.
  • Printing your own: the cost of filament and printer time, often just a few dollars of material, or free booking at a library.
  • Printed parts ordered from Etsy: you pay for filament, print time, and post processing, for riders with no printer access.
  • Pole, LEDs, heat shrink, and hardware are shared with the metal build, and can be ordered a la carte or sourced yourself from the parts list.

Kits and assembly

  • Kit prices follow the parts in the box. Buy one piece or the whole thing, in many configurations, and only pay for what you actually need.
  • Fully assembled adds a flat $30 assembly fee. That pays for the time to print or modify the mount, wrap and seal the pole, wire it, and test it before it ships from Santa Cruz.
  • Shipping is charged at what it costs to get a long, awkward box to you. Sourcing your pole locally is the easiest way to shrink it.
  • Nothing here is a paywall on safety. The free build path stays complete, start to finish.

The tall one

Party Saver

Six feet of rainbow light, straight up. Part totem, part beacon, all joy. On a group ride it marks who is leading and where the party is, visible over cars, crowds, and the whole ride.

Build it yourself

Same idea as the LaneSaber build, scaled up. A quick tube mount with a pinch to hold the pole, an extra long 6 foot pole, and the good rainbow LEDs. Sync a whole club in the same colors and roll as one glowing unit.

Start from the LaneSaber guide

Buy it from the shop

Party Savers and the parts to make one are listed on Etsy when in stock. Built in Santa Cruz, ready for your next Bike Party, critical mass, or night ride.

Shop on Etsy

A level up project, handle with care

Building a Party Saber is much more challenging than the LaneSaber build, and it is possible to damage these LEDs while doing assembly. This is a level up project. Do not put too much pressure on the pins and the solder joints. Basically, if you wrap it too tight, you break it. Wrap gently and take your time.

Party Saber uses a specific LED strip sold on Amazon: Party Saber lights

For the builders

Co-ops, bike kitchens, and clubs

LaneSaber spreads best when a neighborhood builds its own. This page is for the shops and groups who want to run a build night and put a batch on local roads.

Photo coming soon A real build night photo will go here. No AI image is used for this spot.

Run a workshop or build night

  • Order kits or parts in bulk configurations from Etsy, one box per builder, or mix metal and Open Build stations.
  • Builders source poles locally, which keeps shipping low and teaches the sourcing skill too.
  • A good session size is a handful of bikes at a time. Everyone leaves with a mounted, tested LaneSaber.
  • Sell or give away what your group builds, locally, on your own terms. No permission needed.

Get help, remote or in person

  • Remote, anywhere: happy to walk your group through the build over Zoom or Google Meet, tools, jigs, and all the small tricks included.
  • In person: Bay Area only. Beyond that, remote help is how this scales, and it works.
  • Margins, materials, and costs are open too. Ask and they get shared, so your group can price its own builds fairly.

Get workshop kits on Etsy

Good fits for a build night

  • Bike co-ops and bike kitchens with a commuter and cargo bike crowd.
  • Bike buses. Vertical is follow the leader, horizontal is do not pass, and it keeps kids from drifting past the leader on the left.
  • Adaptive, trike, and recumbent groups. A pole up high makes a low rider visible above modern car hoods.
  • Family and cargo bike clubs who ride in real traffic every day.

What happens after

One LaneSaber on a bike in your town starts attracting attention. Drivers learn what it means, riders ask where it came from, and the next build night fills itself. That is the model, town by town, builder by builder.
